title: Family and possession
goal: Name family members, say "my" with the right form, and understand why Icelanders have no family names at all.
bekal: name the members of your close family, including their irregular plurals
use *minn / mín / mitt* and *þinn / þín / þitt* in the right place
read an Icelandic name and know who the person's father is from the name alone

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fjölskyldumyndin
dialogs.intro: A family photo hangs in Anna's living room. Búdí takes a closer look, and his questions lead to an Icelandic custom that surprises him.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Já. Þetta er mamma mín og þetta er pabbi minn.
lines.id: Yes. This is my mom and this is my dad.
lines.literal: yes. this is mom my and this is dad my.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: Do you have brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Ég á eina systur og tvo bræður.
lines.id: I have one sister and two brothers.
lines.literal: I own one sister and two brothers.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Systir mín heitir Guðrún. Bræður mínir heita Jón og Ólafur.
lines.id: My sister is called Guðrún. My brothers are called Jón and Ólafur.
lines.literal: sister my is-called Guðrún. brothers my are-called Jón and Ólafur.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Anna Jónsdóttir … svo pabbi þinn heitir líka Jón?
lines.id: Anna Jónsdóttir… so your dad is called Jón too?
lines.literal: Anna Jónsdóttir… so dad your is-called also Jón?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Rétt! Ég er dóttir Jóns. Bróðir minn heitir Jónsson.
lines.id: Right! I'm Jón's daughter. My brother's last name is Jónsson.
lines.literal: right! I am daughter Jón's. brother my is-called Jónsson.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Svo þið hafið ekki sama eftirnafn?
lines.id: So you don't have the same last name?
lines.literal: so you-all have not same after-name?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nei, við notum ekki ættarnöfn. Í símaskránni erum við undir fornafni.
lines.id: No, we don't use family names. In the phone book we're listed under our first name.
lines.literal: no, we use not family-names. in phone-book-the are we under fore-name.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Merkilegt! Í Indónesíu á ég bara eitt nafn.
lines.id: Interesting! In Indonesia I only have one name.
lines.literal: remarkable! in Indonesia own I only one name.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Þá erum við lík. Nafnið þitt er þitt eigið.
lines.id: Then we're alike. Your name is your very own.
lines.literal: then are we alike. name-the yours is yours own.

notes: **The possessive stands AFTER the noun.** *Mamma mín* = "mom my", *bókin mín* = "book-the my", *nafnið þitt* = "name-the your". English speakers have to flip a lifelong habit (*my mom*); it helps to think "the book of mine".

**And its form follows the gender of the THING owned, not the owner.** *Pabbi **minn*** (*pabbi* is kk), *mamma **mín*** (*mamma* is kvk), *nafnið **mitt*** (*nafn* is hk). What decides is not who owns it but the noun in front.

**Anna Jónsdóttir literally means "Anna, Jón's daughter".** It isn't a family name but a **father's name**. If Anna has a daughter called Sara, the girl becomes *Sara Önnudóttir* or — more often — takes her father's name. Last names change every generation, so no family shares one surname.

**That's why the Icelandic phone book is sorted by FIRST name**, and Icelanders call everyone by their first name — prime minister and president included. Saying *herra Jónsson* ("Mr. Jónsson") actually sounds wrong, because "Jónsson" isn't the person's name.

**Eina systur, tvo bræður — the number and the noun change** because they're the object of *eiga*. The basic forms are *ein systir*, *tveir bræður*. This change is þolfall, and it only gets its name in Unit 8.
**Merkilegt — a neuter adjective used as an exclamation.** Just like *gott!*, *frábært!*, *leiðinlegt!* When there's no clear noun, Icelandic always falls back on the hvorugkyn form.

grammars.title: Minn, þinn — possessives
body: The two most common possessives, each in three forms. Notice the pattern is the same as the adjective pattern in Unit 3.
after: **Only *minn* and *þinn* change form**; the rest stay put. So the load is much lighter than it looks — six forms to learn, not eighteen.
The noun usually takes the **article** unless it's a family word: *bókin mín* (my book), *húsið mitt* (my house). But family members appear bare: *mamma mín*, *pabbi minn*, *systir mín* — no article.
*Bókin hans* means "his book" and *bókin hennar* "her book" — the same split English makes, so here at least nothing new to decide.

grammars.title: Family: singular and plural
body: Family words are among the oldest in Icelandic, and old words are almost always irregular. It's not just the ending that changes but the vowel in the middle — like English *man/men*, *foot/feet*.
after: Note the pattern: **a → e**, **ó → æ**, **o → ö**, **u → y**. This vowel change is called *hljóðvarp* and works throughout Icelandic, not just in family words.
*Pabbi* and *mamma* are the everyday forms; *faðir* and *móðir* are more formal and appear more in writing. In conversation, use *pabbi* and *mamma*.
*Systkini* (hk, plural) means "brothers and sisters" without saying which — like English *siblings*, but an everyday word, not a formal one.

sections.title: Why Icelanders have no family names

blocks.text: The Icelandic naming system is the oldest still alive in Europe: the last name is formed from the **father's name** plus *-son* (son) or *-dóttir* (daughter). It changes every generation, so it isn't a family marker but a marker of **relationship**.

blocks.title: What it means in everyday life
items: **Phone books and lists of any kind are sorted by first name.** If you look up "Jónsson", you won't find anyone.
**Everyone is called by their first name**, including the highest officials. The news refers to the prime minister by first name after the first mention.

**There is an official committee for names** — *Mannanafnanefnd*. A baby's name must be writable in the Icelandic alphabet and able to change form for the cases. Names that don't pass must be changed.
**The mother can be the reference.** *Önnudóttir* (Anna's daughter) is legal and increasingly common, though the father's name is still far more usual.

blocks.text: Búdí finds this familiar for a reason: millions of Indonesians go by **a single name** with no family name at all. In Iceland, too, your first name really is your name.

*Frændi* and *frænka* are used much more broadly than "uncle" and "aunt" in English: they cover uncles, cousins, and other relatives you don't need to spell out. If you need to be precise, name the relationship: *bróðir pabba míns* — my father's brother.

items: The father is Jón, his son is Ólafur → Ólafur ____
The father is Jón, his daughter is Anna → Anna ____
The father is Einar, his daughter is Guðrún → Guðrún ____
The father is Ólafur, his son is Jón → Jón ____
The mother is Anna, her daughter is Sara → Sara ____
This is my dad and this is my mom.
Do you have brothers and sisters?
My name is my very own.
